subject: Banking
title: Identity Theft and Credit Fraud
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Identity Theft and Credit Fraud.

hook.text: Every 22 seconds, someone in the US becomes a victim of identity theft.

buildup.text: Thieves open credit cards, take out loans, and file tax returns using stolen identities.

discovery.text: The dark web sells complete identity kits — name, SSN, address, and mother's maiden name — for as little as $15.

twist.text: Victims bear the burden of proof. You must prove you didn't open the account.

climax.text: Identity theft is cheap to commit and expensive to fix. The criminal profits quickly; the victim suffers for years.

punchline.text: $15 on the dark web buys a full identity. Victims spend months recovering.

quiz.question: How much does a stolen identity cost on the dark web?

details.summary: Identity theft in the credit context occurs when criminals use stolen personal information to open fraudulent accounts, make unauthorized charges, or take out loans in your name, potentially devastating your credit score and financial life.
details.whyItMatters: Identity theft affects millions of Americans annually, costing billions and requiring months to resolve. A single fraudulent account can drop your credit score by 100 points and take years of dispute work to correct.
takeaways: Over 40 million Americans have been victims of identity theft
Criminals use stolen data to open new credit accounts in victims' names
Recovery typically requires months of dispute work across multiple bureaus

faq.question: What should you do first if you discover identity theft?
faq.answer: Place a fraud alert or freeze at all three credit bureaus immediately. File an identity theft report at IdentityTheft.gov. Contact the fraud departments of any compromised accounts. File a police report for documentation purposes.

faq.question: Who is liable for fraudulent charges from identity theft?
faq.answer: Federal law limits your liability. You are not responsible for fraudulent accounts opened in your name. Unauthorized credit card charges are capped at $50, and most issuers waive even that. But cleaning up the mess takes significant time and effort.
